en.title: The longue durée of social change
en.summary: PART XV turns from sectoral and period-specific analysis to synthesis. Chapter 143 asks what becomes visible when the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga is examined across very long spans of time rather than divided into isolated ancient, medieval, colonial and contemporary compartments. The term longue durée is useful only if it does not flatten change.

mai.title: सामाजिक परिवर्तनक दीर्घकाल
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “सामाजिक परिवर्तनक दीर्घकाल” विषयक दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Longue durée is a scale of analysis, not a claim that society stood still
Environment shaped possibilities without mechanically determining society
The shift from mobile subsistence to settled production created new social dependencies
Early historic urbanisation multiplied institutions rather than replacing the countryside

en.title: From Subsistence to Market Integration
en.summary: Chapter 144 synthesises the long economic movement from household provisioning and locally bounded exchange toward increasingly dense regional, national and cross-border markets. The phrase 'from subsistence to market integration' must not be read as a ladder on which self-provisioning disappears as markets advance. In Mithila, Vajji and Anga, households have repeatedly combined food production, reciprocal labour, craft, wage work, tenancy, migration, remittances and trade.

mai.title: आत्मनिर्वाहसँ बजार-एकीकरणधरि
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “आत्मनिर्वाहसँ बजार-एकीकरणधरि” विषयक दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Subsistence and market exchange are overlapping strategies, not opposite stages
Ecological diversity created multiple pathways into exchange
Storage transformed surplus into a social and economic resource
Early towns linked agrarian surplus to specialised labour and institutions

en.title: Household, Caste, Class and Gender across Time
en.summary: Chapter 145 synthesises one of the central arguments of this volume: household, caste, class and gender are not separate topics that can be stacked beside one another. They are overlapping institutions through which land, labour, marriage, care, education, mobility, status and political claims are organised. Yet none of them is timeless.

mai.title: समयक पार घर-परिवार, जाति, वर्ग आ लैंगिकता
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “समयक पार घर-परिवार, जाति, वर्ग आ लैंगिकता” विषयक दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Household, family, lineage and kin group are not interchangeable
Early evidence permits reconstruction of social relations more securely than a complete household model
Kinship became an economic institution because marriage redistributed people, property and obligations
Property is one of the principal channels through which household power becomes durable

en.title: Riverine Ecology and Economic History
en.summary: Chapter 146 synthesises a proposition that runs through the entire volume: rivers are not a background to the history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga. They are active ecological and economic institutions. Himalayan rivers bring water and sediment, create and erase land, recharge wetlands, interrupt roads, sustain fisheries, shape cropping calendars and repeatedly redistribute settlement.

mai.title: नदीय पारिस्थितिकी आ आर्थिक इतिहास
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “नदीय पारिस्थितिकी आ आर्थिक इतिहास” विषयक दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Rivers made the alluvial plains that later societies inhabited
Flood is a hydrological event; disaster is a social relationship
Seasonal water pulses organised agricultural time
Silt is both fertility and obstruction

en.title: Language as Social Infrastructure
en.summary: Chapter 147 synthesises a central argument of this volume: language is not only a marker of identity or a vehicle of literature. It is infrastructure through which households coordinate care, markets exchange information, schools transmit knowledge, courts and administrations communicate rights, migrants maintain relationships, and digital systems make people visible or invisible. Roads connect places; language connects intentions, rules, memories and transactions.

mai.title: सामाजिक आधारभूत संरचना रूपमे भाषा
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “सामाजिक आधारभूत संरचना रूपमे भाषा” विषयक दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Language infrastructure begins with coordination, not with official status
Multilingualism is the normal condition of the region, not an exception
Oral language carried institutions long before mass literacy
Script converted speech into durable records but also created gatekeepers

en.title: India and Nepal: One Interaction Zone, Multiple Political Economies
en.summary: Chapter 148 synthesises the cross-border argument developed throughout this volume. Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be reconstructed adequately by treating the India–Nepal boundary as either an impermeable line or an irrelevant modern interruption. The border separates two sovereign states with different constitutions, currencies, taxation systems, welfare regimes, regulatory institutions and macroeconomic structures.

mai.title: भारत आ नेपाल: एक परस्पर क्रिया-क्षेत्र, अनेक राजनीतिक अर्थव्यवस्था
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “भारत आ नेपाल: एक परस्पर क्रिया-क्षेत्र, अनेक राजनीतिक अर्थव्यवस्था” विषयक दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: An interaction zone is a field of repeated connection, not a claim of political unity
Long before the modern boundary, plains and foothills were linked by rivers, routes and settlement
The 1950 treaty framework institutionalised an unusually open field of movement
Economic asymmetry is structural, but dependence is not one-directional

en.title: Cultural Persistence, Reinvention and Modern Institutions
en.summary: Chapter 149 synthesises a central argument of this volume: cultural persistence is not the survival of an unchanged substance from an imagined timeless past. Practices endure because people repeatedly reproduce them under altered ecological, political, economic and technological conditions.

mai.title: सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरता, पुनर्रचना आ आधुनिक संस्थान
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरता, पुनर्रचना आ आधुनिक संस्थान” विषयक दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Persistence is active reproduction, not passive survival
Reinvention is one mechanism of continuity
The household remains the smallest durable cultural institution
Public ritual turns cultural persistence into civic negotiation

en.title: Conclusion: Socio-Cultural-Economic Histories without Timeless Essences
en.summary: Chapter 150 closes Volume II by drawing together the argument developed across the preceding 149 chapters. The history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga cannot be written as the biography of an unchanging civilisation, a fixed caste order, a single linguistic community, a continuous political unit or a timeless cultural personality.

mai.title: निष्कर्ष: कालातीत सार बिना सामाजिक-सांस्कृतिक-आर्थिक इतिहास
mai.summary: ई अध्याय दीर्घकालिक सामाजिक परिवर्तन, बजार, परिवार-जाति-वर्ग-लैंगिकता, नदी, भाषा, भारत-नेपाल सम्बन्ध आ सांस्कृतिक निरन्तरताक मुख्य निष्कर्ष समेटि मिथ्या कालातीत एकरूपताक बदला ऐतिहासिक सम्बन्ध, परिवर्तन आ भिन्नता स्पष्ट करैत अछि।

outline: The region is historical because its boundaries and connections changed
Ecology is a historical agent without becoming environmental determinism
Settlement history undermines the myth of an eternally village-bound society
Agrarian continuity coexisted with repeated changes in property, labour and technology
